Digestion, Lymph and Immunity, Hormones, Kidneys, Reproduction, and Blood Terms

Unit 1: Anatomy and Physiology. Lesson 7 of 60 in CBET Academy.

The remaining body systems, at the depth the exam asks: the organ, its job, and the one fact that gets tested.

The digestive tract, in order

Digestion is movement, secretion, chemical breakdown, and absorption.

  1. Mouth: chewing (mastication) increases surface area; salivary amylase starts on starch and lingual lipase on fat.
  2. Esophagus: the epiglottis covers the airway during swallowing; the lower esophageal sphincter keeps acid out of the esophagus.
  3. Stomach: grinds food and adds gastric acid (pH about 1.5 to 3.5) and proteases; the pyloric sphincter releases the resulting chyme slowly.
  4. Small intestine: duodenum (first section, most chemical digestion, receives bile and pancreatic enzymes), jejunum (absorbs sugars, amino acids, fatty acids), ileum (finishes absorption, recovers bile salts).
  5. Large intestine: reabsorbs water to form solid waste; hosts bacteria that make vitamin K.

Accessory organs: the liver (largest solid organ; makes bile, plasma proteins, and cholesterol; stores glucose as glycogen; converts ammonia to urea; clears drugs and toxins; regulates clotting), the gallbladder (stores and concentrates bile, releases it into the duodenum), and the pancreas (exocrine digestive enzymes into the duodenum; endocrine insulin and glucagon into the blood).

Lymphatic and immune systems

The lymphatic system drains interstitial fluid as lymph through vessels with valves, filters it in lymph nodes (concentrated in the neck, armpits, and groin), and returns it to the veins through lymphatic ducts. Lymphoid tissues: tonsils, the thymus (where T cells mature), the spleen (cleans blood of old cells and pathogens), and Peyer's patches in the small intestine. The immune system uses white cells and antibodies to avoid, detect, and eliminate infection; it does not filter toxins (the kidneys do that) and is not controlled by the hypothalamus.

Endocrine glands and feedback

Hormones travel in blood and act only on cells with matching receptors. The hypothalamus and pituitary form the control center. Glands to know: thyroid (metabolic rate), parathyroid (four small glands on the posterior of the thyroid's lateral lobes; raise blood calcium), adrenal cortex (cortisol, salt and sugar balance) and adrenal medulla (epinephrine), pancreatic islets (insulin lowers glucose, glucagon raises it), thymus, pineal (daily rhythms), and the gonads. Most regulation is negative feedback: rising glucose triggers insulin, which lowers glucose, which stops the trigger. Positive feedback amplifies (labor contractions). The pons is brain stem, not a gland.

The kidney, closer up

Each kidney has an outer renal cortex, inner renal medulla, and a renal pelvis that funnels urine into the ureter. About a million nephrons do the work: blood enters the glomerulus (a capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule), where blood pressure drives filtration; the filtrate runs through tubules that reabsorb water, glucose, and ions, secrete wastes and hydrogen ions (adjusting pH), and send the rest to collecting ducts as urine. Urine leaves through the ureters, the bladder, and the urethra. Dialysis imitates the nephron with a membrane and dialysate.

Reproduction

Male: testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm mature in the epididymis, travel the vas deferens, and mix with fluids from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands. Hormones: FSH drives sperm production, LH drives testosterone. Female: ovaries make eggs and secrete estrogen and progesterone; the egg travels the fallopian tube, where fertilization occurs, and the embryo implants in the uterus; the vagina is the birth canal.

Blood terms that get confused

Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red cells that carries oxygen. Hematocrit is the fraction of blood volume that is red cells (about 45 percent), measured by spinning a sample in a hematocrit centrifuge. An adult has about 5 liters (five quarts) of blood. White cell types: lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils. Red cells live about four months and have no nucleus.

Exam tip: the duodenum is the first part of the small intestine; the large intestine reabsorbs water; the gallbladder stores bile and the liver makes it; the pancreas makes insulin. Fertilization is in the fallopian tube. Filtration in the kidney is driven by blood pressure. Hemoglobin carries oxygen; hematocrit is the red-cell fraction. Negative feedback keeps things stable.
Remember
Mouth amylase and lipase, epiglottis, stomach pH 1.5 to 3.5, pyloric sphincter, chyme, duodenum then jejunum then ileum, large intestine reabsorbs water. Liver makes bile, glycogen, urea; gallbladder stores bile; pancreas enzymes and insulin. Lymph nodes, tonsils, thymus, spleen, Peyer's patches. Parathyroid on the back of the thyroid raises calcium; negative feedback. Cortex, medulla, pelvis; glomerulus in Bowman's capsule; blood pressure drives filtration. Fertilization in the fallopian tube. Hemoglobin carries oxygen, hematocrit is the red-cell fraction, about 5 liters.
Deeper explanation

Digestion, Lymph and Immunity, Hormones, Kidneys, Reproduction, and Blood Terms, explained slowly

The rest of the body, room by room

These systems are tested with one or two facts each, usually a function-to-organ match. Use the digestive tract as a conveyor belt with stations, the kidney as a filter plant, the endocrine system as a thermostat network, and the lymphatic system as the building's drainage.

The conveyor belt

station            action                                          enzyme or chemical
mouth              mastication; starch and fat digestion begin      salivary amylase, lingual lipase
esophagus          swallowing; epiglottis guards the airway         lower esophageal sphincter blocks reflux
stomach            grinding; protein digestion; storage             gastric acid pH 1.5 to 3.5, proteases; pyloric sphincter meters chyme out
duodenum           first small-intestine section; chemical digestion; absorption begins   receives bile and pancreatic enzymes
jejunum            absorbs sugars, amino acids, fatty acids
ileum              finishes absorption; reclaims bile salts
large intestine    reabsorbs water; forms solid waste               resident bacteria make vitamin K

Accessory organs: liver (bile production, plasma proteins, cholesterol, glycogen storage, urea from ammonia, detoxification, clotting regulation, immune support), gallbladder (stores and concentrates bile; releases it to the duodenum), pancreas (exocrine enzymes; endocrine insulin and glucagon). Secretin and cholecystokinin are duodenal hormones, not gallbladder products.

Drainage and defense

Interstitial fluid enters lymph capillaries, becomes lymph, is filtered in nodes (neck, armpits, groin), and returns to the veins through ducts; valves and muscle contraction move it. Lymphoid tissue: tonsils (throat), thymus (T-cell school), spleen (blood cleaner), Peyer's patches (intestine). The immune system's job is to avoid, detect, and eliminate infection. Two things it does not do: filter toxins (kidneys) and make blood cells on hormonal command (the kidney's erythropoietin does that).

The thermostat network

gland               secretes                    effect
hypothalamus        releasing hormones          commands the pituitary
pituitary           growth and control hormones master gland
thyroid             thyroxine                   metabolic rate, growth
parathyroid         parathyroid hormone         raises blood calcium; four glands on the posterior lateral lobes of the thyroid
adrenal cortex      cortisol, aldosterone       sugar, salt, stress
adrenal medulla     epinephrine                 heart rate, blood sugar, vessel size
pancreatic islets   insulin, glucagon           lower and raise blood glucose
thymus              thymosin                    immune maturation
pineal              melatonin                   daily rhythms
gonads              estrogen, progesterone, testosterone

Negative feedback: the response cancels the stimulus (insulin after a meal). Positive feedback: the response amplifies the stimulus (oxytocin in labor). The pons is part of the brain stem and secretes nothing.

The filter plant

structure                   role
renal cortex                outer layer; holds the glomeruli
renal medulla               inner layer; collecting ducts
renal pelvis                funnel to the ureter
nephron (about a million)   the working unit
glomerulus in Bowman's capsule   capillary tuft where blood pressure forces filtrate out
proximal tubule             reabsorbs water, glucose, ions
distal tubule               secretes wastes and hydrogen ions (pH control)
collecting duct             final concentration; urine to the pelvis
ureter, bladder, urethra    transport, storage, exit

Filtration is driven by blood pressure, not osmosis or muscle. Dialysis reproduces the membrane step.

Reproduction, in one table

male                                          female
testes: sperm and testosterone                ovaries: eggs, estrogen, progesterone
epididymis stores; vas deferens carries       fallopian tube: fertilization happens here
seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral fluids   uterus: implantation and gestation
FSH drives sperm production; LH drives testosterone   vagina: receives sperm, birth canal

Blood terms

Hemoglobin is the iron protein that binds oxygen inside red cells; hematocrit is the red-cell fraction of blood volume (about 45 percent), read after spinning a capillary tube; total volume is about 5 liters. White cells: lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils; platelets clot; plasma is the water and proteins.

How the exam asks it

  • "The large intestine ___." Reabsorbs water into the body to form solid waste.
  • "What does the gallbladder secrete into the GI tract?" Bile.
  • "Where is the parathyroid gland?" On the lateral lobes of the thyroid, posterior aspect.
  • "Insulin release falling as glucose falls is an example of?" Negative feedback.
  • "Which does not produce hormones: pituitary, pons, pancreas, ovaries?" Pons.
  • "The primary driver of filtration in the kidneys?" Blood pressure.
  • "Which statement about hemoglobin is wrong?" That it is the ratio of red cells to blood volume (that is hematocrit).
  • "Fertilization occurs in the?" Fallopian tubes.

What to memorize

  • The conveyor belt in order with its enzymes and the pH of the stomach; duodenum first, jejunum second, ileum third; large intestine reabsorbs water.
  • Liver makes bile, gallbladder stores it, pancreas makes insulin and enzymes.
  • Lymph nodes filter; thymus, spleen, tonsils, Peyer's patches.
  • Parathyroid raises calcium on the back of the thyroid; negative feedback stabilizes.
  • Cortex, medulla, pelvis; glomerulus, Bowman's capsule; blood pressure filters.
  • Fallopian tube fertilization; FSH and LH.
  • Hemoglobin carries, hematocrit is the fraction, five liters.
